# Comparing the method with cities that already tax {#sec-calibration}

```{r}
#| include: false
source(here::here("chapters", "_common.R"))
```

## What was done

Eighteen New York cities already have their own sales tax, so for each of them a second estimate of the taxable base exists: the city's collections divided by its rate. The identical division of the county base described in @sec-apportionment was run on those cities and compared with that second estimate. Seventeen reconcile with their counties' figures (Oswego does not; see @sec-policy). Two, Salamanca and Ogdensburg, are set aside for documented reasons that do not apply to Albany: the whole of Salamanca sits on the Seneca Nation's territory, where most retail is outside the tax base, and Ogdensburg's reporting code was created in 2022 and its collections are still catching up. Fifteen cities remain.

Before the collections-based figure was used it was tested. At the county level, where both quantities are published, collections divided by rate reproduces reported taxable sales within a few percent in every county over three years. Each city's inferred share of its county is stable from year to year. The year a city adopted its tax does not predict how it compares. And resampling counties rather than cities, to allow for cities in the same county missing together, gives the same ranges. The detail is in @sec-city-detail.

## What we conclude

- For the typical taxing city, collections come in about **`r fp(1 - R$gm_pref, 0)` below** the base the division of the county figure gives. The scatter around that is about `r sd_up(fit_pref$sigma)` on the high side and `r sd_dn(fit_pref$sigma)` on the low side for a typical city.
- The reasons are identifiable and mostly apply to Albany too: vendors reporting sales under the county's code rather than the city's; large taxable purchasers outside cities (plants, resorts, data centres) that a jobs-based rule cannot see; Economic Census receipts being gross rather than taxable; and exempt hospitals and universities inside cities.
- How the comparison is turned into an adjustment matters. Netting out county size, the adjustment is that single `r fp(1 - R$gm_pref, 0)`. A line fitted in dollar levels scales Albany down by more, because the large-county cities in the sample (the four in Westchester) have low ratios; whether that would apply to Albany County is a judgment. Both readings are reported in @sec-results.
- **The comparison is examined closely and given limited weight.** The collections-based base is itself an estimate, made from a rate that had to be verified city by city and from cash that cannot distinguish a sale coded to the county from one that never happened. Fifteen cities, in eleven counties, cannot settle much. The central estimate uses the typical gap because the city would be paid on collections; the apportioned base with no adjustment is reported alongside it as a reading in its own right.

## How it is used

The central estimate in @sec-results is the apportioned base reduced by the typical gap. The range comes from the scatter of the fifteen cities around that gap, widened for the uncertainty in the gap itself. The planning range adds the readings under every plausible specification, including no adjustment at all. The only thing that would replace this comparison is a tabulation of taxable sales inside the city limits from the Tax Department, which holds city-coded returns but does not publish them (@sec-data).

## The shopping response

The add-on makes the rate 8.5% inside the city against 8.0% outside, a 0.46% change in the tax-inclusive price at the city line. Vehicles are unaffected (sourced to residence). Business purchases, utilities and most services do not move. Only the over-the-counter classes, `r fp(R$store_share_of_base, 0)` of the base, are mobile at all, and only near the boundary. The central estimate assumes no loss. A shopping response would also have a second, smaller effect that the estimate sets to zero along with the first: a sale that moves out of the city is still taxed by the county, but one that moves out of the county is not, and the city's population-based share of county collections would fall with it; even if every dollar of a 3% loss on the store classes left the county, that second effect would be worth about \$`r fm(R$beta_second_order, 2)` million a year. The research on cross-border shopping (Agrawal 2015; Baker, Johnson and Kueng 2021) establishes that responses exist and concentrate near rate boundaries, but neither study measures a half-point difference inside one county, so the lower cases in @sec-sensitivity are illustrative. Note the units: a 3% loss of base against a 6.25% rise in the tax is an elasticity of about 0.5 with respect to the *rate*, but against the tax-inclusive price, which rises only 0.46%, it is an elasticity of about 6.5, which would be a large response, not a modest one.
